h1: Moving from a brewpub to a large brewery
title: Moving from a Brewpub to a Large Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: What changes when a brewpub brewer joins a large brewery in India: scale, shifts, automation, procedures and the skills that transfer.
teaser: In a brewpub you do everything. In a large brewery you do one thing, very precisely, on a shift.
standfirst: Brewpub brewers sometimes move to large breweries for structure, training or a broader career path. The move is a big change in scale and culture. Knowing what to expect makes the first year far easier.
sections:
A typical Indian brewpub runs a brewhouse of a few hectolitres, often in the range of 5 to 10 hl, with a handful of fermenters. A large brewery may brew several batches a day on brewhouses of hundreds of hectolitres, with fermentation tanks many times larger and packaging lines filling tens of thousands of bottles or cans an hour.

At that scale small errors become expensive. A one degree mistake in a fermentation tank affects thousands of litres. A wrong valve opened during a transfer can send beer to drain. The process is built to prevent those mistakes. Much of your first months will be spent learning those safeguards.

In a brewpub one brewer may mill, mash, boil, clean, ferment, filter, keg and serve. In a large brewery those are separate jobs and often separate teams: brewhouse, fermentation and cellars, filtration, packaging, utilities and quality. You will usually join one area and rotate later.

That can feel narrow at first. The upside is depth. You learn one area thoroughly, with proper training and experienced colleagues. Our guide on shift brewer at a large brewery describes a typical role in detail.

Large breweries run on automated control systems. Mash temperatures, transfers, cleaning cycles and fermentation profiles are often controlled from a screen. Your job shifts from doing the work by hand to monitoring the process, responding to alarms and stepping in when something drifts.

This needs different skills: reading trend graphs, understanding interlocks and knowing what the system is doing behind the screen. Brewpub brewers often bring a real advantage here, because they know what is physically happening in the tank when the screen shows a number.

Large breweries operate under written standard operating procedures, food safety systems such as HACCP and often certifications such as ISO 22000 or FSSC 22000. Every batch is recorded. Every deviation is logged and investigated. Every change goes through an approval process.

Brewpub brewers used to adjusting things on the fly can find this frustrating. It helps to understand why. When one batch fills a large number of bottles, consistency and traceability are what protect the brand. Follow the procedure first. Suggest improvements through the proper route.
Shifts and safety are part of the job

Many large breweries run round the clock, especially in summer. Expect rotating shifts, including nights and weekends. Handovers between shifts are formal, with written logs.

Safety rules are strict too. Permits to work, lockout and tagout on equipment, confined space entry procedures for tanks and personal protective equipment for caustic and acid are standard. These rules exist because people have been hurt. Brewpubs often run more loosely, so take the safety induction seriously.
What carries over from the brewpub

More than you might think. You understand the whole process, end to end, which many specialists in large plants do not. You can taste problems, you know how yeast behaves and you are used to solving problems with limited resources. You have also probably done more cleaning than anyone, which is the backbone of any brewery.

Brewpub brewers often adapt well to troubleshooting roles once they learn the systems. Those who later move back to craft, as described in moving from a large brewery to a craft brewery, often bring the best of both worlds.

Large breweries will test your process knowledge, safety awareness and ability to follow procedures. Be ready to explain how you clean a fermenter, how you check a fermentation is complete and how you would handle a deviation. Mention any experience with HACCP, records or quality checks.

Show you understand the trade-off: less variety, more precision. If you can talk about lager fermentation at around 8 to 13 °C, diacetyl rests and consistent final gravity across batches, you will sound ready for a plant that makes the same beer every day.

Write down every task you did in your last full brewpub week. Next to each, write what a large brewery would do differently: who would do it, what system would control it and what record would be kept. That exercise shows you where you are already strong and where the learning will be.
faqs: Is it hard to move from a brewpub to a large brewery?
It is a big change in scale and culture, but very doable. Expect specialisation, automation, formal procedures and shift work.
Will my brewpub experience count at a large brewery?
Yes. End-to-end process knowledge, tasting skills and practical troubleshooting are valued, especially once you learn the plant systems.
Many do, often around the clock in peak season, with rotating shifts and formal handovers.
Following written procedures exactly and making changes through formal approval rather than adjusting things on the fly.
